title: 1680: The Revolt That Worked
description: The Pueblo Revolt of 1680: the Acoma backstory, the causes, Popé's village-by-village organization, twelve years of freedom, and what it proved about Indigenous agency and the limits of empire.
essential_question: Why did the Pueblo Revolt succeed where other resistance failed?
learning_objectives: Identify the causes of the Pueblo Revolt: mission labor, drought, and religious repression.
Describe how Popé organized the revolt across Pueblo villages.
Explain what the revolt's success shows about Indigenous agency and the limits of empire.

key_terms.definition: The 1680 Pueblo uprising led by Popé that expelled the Spanish from New Mexico for twelve years.
A Pueblo religious leader who organized the 1680 revolt village by village.
The Spanish colonial institution that combined religious conversion with coerced Indigenous labor.

presentation.tone: a teacher talking to a smart 16-year-old; plain, spoken, concrete

narration.text: [solemn]In August 1680, in the deserts of New Mexico, the Spanish Empire lost a war to people it had already beaten. The Pueblo peoples rose up, killed hundreds of colonists, burned the churches, and drove the Spanish out completely. [beat] It is the only Native revolt in North American history that threw the colonizers out entirely. And the Pueblos held their country for twelve years.

narration.text: [solemn]To understand 1680, start eighty years earlier. In [date:1598], the conquistador Juan de Oñate occupied the mesa fortress of Acoma Pueblo. When the Acoma refused to hand over winter supplies, they killed fifteen Spaniards, including Oñate's nephew. [beat] Oñate answered with cannons. More than eight hundred Acoma died. The man who ordered it was Oñate himself, governor of New Mexico.

narration.text: The terror worked, for a while. For eighty years the Pueblos lived under Spanish rule, and the pressure built. [beat] The missions demanded labor in the fields while priests punished Pueblo ceremonies as witchcraft. Drought starved the villages in the 1670s. Then in [date:1675], the governor arrested forty-seven Pueblo religious leaders. Three were hanged. The rest were whipped. [beat] Among the survivors was a man named [es]Popé[/es].

narration.text: [es]Popé[/es] fled north to Taos Pueblo, beyond the Spanish reach. And there he did what no one had done before: he united the villages. [beat] Look at this cord. Knots tied along its length. What is it for? [2s pause] It is a calendar, and a battle plan. Runners carried cords like this from village to village. Each morning the leaders untied one knot. When the last knot came undone, every village would rise on the same day.

narration.text: [fierce]On August 10, [date:1680], the knots ran out. Across New Mexico, Pueblo warriors attacked at once. They killed more than three hundred Spaniards, including twenty-one of the thirty-three Franciscan priests. They burned the churches and besieged Santa Fe. [beat] The survivors fled south to El Paso. New Mexico belonged to the Pueblos again.

narration.text: [solemn]For twelve years, the Pueblos governed themselves. They tore down the missions and danced the old dances in the open. [beat] When the Spanish returned in [date:1692], they came back changed. They appointed a defender for Pueblo rights, granted Pueblo families land, and stopped trying to crush the old religion. [beat] The revolt had worked. It proved that Indigenous people could defeat a European empire, and it forced that empire to rule differently.
